title: How to Skate in the Wind on Inline Speed Skates
thumbnail_text: Why a headwind feels so brutal, and the fix

scenes.heading: How to Skate in the Wind
scenes.sub: Position, stroke and route fixes for windy days
scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will know how to skate into a headwind, through a crosswind, and with a tailwind. You will also know how to plan a windy day route so the wind helps you when you are tired. Wind is the road condition skaters complain about most and prepare for least. A steady headwind quietly flattens your average speed. It can make you wonder whether your bearings are dying. They probably are not. Here is what the wind is really doing, and what you can change about it.

scenes.heading: What a headwind really costs you
bullets: Drag rises with the square of airspeed
Fast skaters pay far more than slow ones
Your watch shows ground speed, not airspeed
Expensive work at a cheap speed
scenes.narration: Air resistance climbs with the square of the speed you move through the air. Double the airspeed and the drag is roughly four times greater. That is why a headwind punishes fast skaters far more than slow ones. Now the key point. Your watch measures speed over the ground. The air only cares about your speed through the air. Skate at 25 kilometres per hour into a 15 kilometres per hour wind, and the air pushes back as hard as it would at 40. But you only get 25 of ground speed for that effort. You are doing expensive work at a cheap speed. That mismatch explains the two classic mistakes. Skaters either chase their usual average until they blow up, or they abandon the session.

scenes.heading: Bending the knees is not getting low
scenes.narration: This diagram shows two skaters. The one on the left has plenty of knee bend, but the chest still faces the wind. The one on the right has dropped the chest toward the thigh, so the torso presents far less area to the air. That is the difference between bending your knees and actually getting low. The drawing is schematic and not to scale, but the idea holds. Frontal area is the biggest variable you control, and you control it with your hips and your back, not your wallet.

scenes.heading: Position comes first, and it is free
bullets: Drop your chest toward your thigh
Flatten your back
Tuck your head in line with your back
Carry one arm on the back
Keep the recovery leg tight
scenes.narration: Before you think about equipment, fix your shape. Drop your chest closer to your thigh. Flatten your back, because a hunched upper back makes a shelf the wind stacks up against. Tuck your head so your helmet sits in line with your back, with your eyes still up the road. Carry one arm on the back, since two wide swinging arms add width exactly where you cannot afford it. And keep the recovery tight, so a trailing leg does not give the air another surface. If this low shape makes your lower back complain within minutes, it is often a mobility and strength limit, and off skate work helps. But if the pain is sharp, spreads into a leg, comes with numbness, or lasts several days, see a doctor or a physiotherapist before you train through it.

scenes.heading: What to do with your stroke
bullets: Shorten the stroke
Raise the cadence, like an easier gear
Keep the push sideways
Never stand up tall into the wind
scenes.narration: The instinct in a headwind is to push harder and longer. That is the wrong instinct. A long, slow, heavily loaded push is where skaters stall, because your leg runs out of force before the glide ends. Instead, shorten the stroke and raise the cadence. More pushes per minute, each slightly less loaded, so the leg keeps cycling. Think of it as dropping into an easier gear. The wind steals your glide, so stop paying for it. Set the skate down, push, recover, repeat. Keep the push sideways, because a push that drifts backwards wastes effort you cannot spare. And do not stand up for a breather. Standing tall into a headwind is like opening a parachute. If you need to recover, recover low and soft.

scenes.heading: Gusts land at the gaps
scenes.narration: A headwind makes you slow. A crosswind can put you on the floor. This diagram shows why gaps matter. Wind speeds up as it squeezes through a gap between buildings, past the end of a wall, or at a bridge or flyover. So the shove lands right at the gap, where you have the least space. On the approach, ease the effort and leave room on both sides. In any crosswind, stay boring. Get low so the wind has less leverage, keep your weight centred, and cut out long one footed glides. Leave a wider buffer from the kerb and traffic, and keep a hand free to balance, because on a gusty day the wind picks your line, not you.

scenes.heading: A tailwind flatters you
bullets: A tailwind best is not real progress
Test fitness on calm days or out and back
Use the tailwind for overspeed work
Short efforts at very high cadence
scenes.narration: Wind behind you is lovely and slightly dishonest. Your average jumps and your legs feel strong, but your fitness did not change this morning. So a tailwind personal best is not evidence of progress. Test yourself on a calm day, or over an out and back route that covers both directions. Better still, use the tailwind on purpose. It is the one time the road lets you hold a very high leg speed without drag capping you. That makes it the best place on your loop for overspeed work. Do short efforts at a cadence above anything you could hold into the wind, and teach your legs to turn over quickly.

scenes.heading: Headwind out, tailwind home
scenes.narration: The best decision on a windy day happens before you leave. This diagram shows an out and back route. Take the headwind leg first, while you are fresh, and come home with the wind behind you. It feels backwards, but the wind does not get easier later, and your legs definitely get worse. Being stranded far from home into a headwind on empty legs is how skaters end up walking. Pick loops with shelter, like tree lined roads or stretches behind a wall, and save your hard efforts for those. On very windy days, drop the long open stretches and use a smaller sheltered loop, even if it means repeats.

scenes.heading: Which gear earns its place in wind
bullets: Position is the biggest gain, and free
A close fitting suit beats a flapping tee
Clean bearings remove a variable
Bigger wheels do not fight the wind
Wear gloves and a well fitted helmet
scenes.narration: This is where skaters lose money. Wind resistance is about your shape and your clothing. Bearings and wheels are a separate loss that matters less once the air takes over. A lower, flatter position is the biggest gain, and it costs nothing. A close fitting race suit instead of a loose tee is a real gain, because loose fabric flaps like a sail. That is why a LiveLica Pro Skin Suit is worth wearing for a hard windy session. Clean, well oiled bearings help the whole ride but do not fight the wind. They simply let you know the air is what is slowing you. A bigger wheel does not help either. And gusty days are when you are most likely to get put down, so wear the gloves you keep skipping, and snug your helmet fit before you drop low.

scenes.heading: Judge the session by time and effort
scenes.chapter: Numbers and a windy day session
bullets: Ignore average speed on windy days
Hold effort constant, let pace drop
Six times two minutes hard into the wind
Overspeed sprints with the wind behind
scenes.narration: Average speed is the wrong measure in wind. Skate for the time you planned, at the effort you planned, and let the distance land where it lands. In intervals, hold the effort and let the pace drop. On easy days, hold an easy breathing rate even if that feels slow, because wind is how an easy day quietly turns hard. Here is a session worth doing. Warm up for fifteen minutes easy. Then do six repeats of two minutes hard on the exposed half, low and quick, ignoring speed, with the sheltered half easy as recovery. Finish with ten minutes easy and, if you still have legs, four sprints of about fifteen seconds with the wind behind you, thinking fast feet.

scenes.heading: When to call it off
bullets: Gusts shift you sideways between strokes
Traffic and no predictable line
Debris or heavy dust in the air
Breathing trouble that does not settle
scenes.narration: Some days are not training days. Shorten the loop, move indoors or stay home when gusts shift you sideways between strokes, when you cannot hold a predictable line in traffic, or when debris, branches or dust are blowing across the road. Be stricter still on broken tarmac, because a gust on a bad patch is far worse than either alone. Protect your airways and eyes too. If a dusty windy session leaves you coughing, wheezy or with sore eyes for more than a day or two, or you get chest tightness or breathlessness that does not settle with rest, see a doctor before you train through it.

scenes.heading: Get low, spin fast, head out into the wind
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you remember one thing, make it this. Into the wind, get lower and narrower, shorten your stroke, and judge the day by effort and time, not average speed. Then head out into the wind and come home with it behind you. The full guide on the LiveLica blog includes a windy day checklist and answers to common questions about wheels, pack racing and arm position. The link is in the description.
